agents.description: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions.

content.text:
# Reading a Tide Table

A tide table lists the predicted times and heights of successive high and low tides for a given location. Each entry is a timestamped prediction, usually spaced roughly 6 to 12.5 hours apart, because most coastlines experience two high tides and two low tides per day (a semidiurnal pattern). To read one correctly, pair the time with its tide type and height, and note the reference datum the heights are measured against — usually Mean Lower Low Water (MLLW) in the US or Chart Datum elsewhere.

## Key Things to Check

When reading any tide table, confirm these details before relying on it:

- **Station and date** — tables are location-specific; a few miles of coastline can shift times by 30+ minutes.
- **Time zone** — check whether times are local, standard, or UTC, and whether daylight saving is applied.
- **Datum** — the zero-height reference point; heights below datum are shown as negative.
- **Tide type** — each row is marked High (H) or Low (L).
- **Height units** — meters or feet, which changes how you interpret magnitude.
- **Range** — the difference between consecutive high and low heights, useful for boating clearance and beach exposure.

## Computing the Next High Tide

Given a list of predicted tide events, you can programmatically find the next upcoming high tide relative to the current time:

```javascript
function getNextHighTide(tides, now = new Date()) {
  // tides: [{ time: "2020-01-06T08:14:00Z", type: "H", height: 1.8 }, ...]
  const upcoming = tides
    .filter(t => t.type === "H")
    .map(t => ({ ...t, time: new Date(t.time) }))
    .filter(t => t.time > now)
    .sort((a, b) => a.time - b.time);

  if (upcoming.length === 0) {
    return null;
  }

  return upcoming[0];
}

const sampleTides = [
  { time: "2020-01-06T02:10:00Z", type: "L", height: 0.3 },
  { time: "2020-01-06T08:14:00Z", type: "H", height: 1.8 },
  { time: "2020-01-06T14:45:00Z", type: "L", height: 0.4 },
  { time: "2020-01-06T20:52:00Z", type: "H", height: 1.9 },
];

const next = getNextHighTide(sampleTides);
console.log(next ? `Next high tide: ${next.time}` : "No more high tides today");
```

This logic filters for high-tide rows, discards any already in the past, and sorts chronologically to return the soonest match — the same approach a tide app uses under the hood.

## Example Table

| Date       | Time  | Type | Height (m) |
|------------|-------|------|------------|
| 2020-01-06 | 02:10 | L    | 0.3        |
| 2020-01-06 | 08:14 | H    | 1.8        |
| 2020-01-06 | 14:45 | L    | 0.4        |
| 2020-01-06 | 20:52 | H    | 1.9        |
| 2020-01-07 | 02:58 | L    | 0.3        |
| 2020-01-07 | 09:05 | H    | 1.7        |
| 2020-01-07 | 15:30 | L    | 0.5        |
| 2020-01-07 | 21:40 | H    | 1.8        |
| 2020-01-08 | 03:42 | L    | 0.4        |
| 2020-01-08 | 09:52 | H    | 1.6        |
| 2020-01-08 | 16:12 | L    | 0.6        |

Reading across a row tells you exactly when and how high the water will rise or fall, while reading down a column reveals the drifting rhythm of the tide — each day's events shift later by roughly 40–50 minutes due to the lunar cycle.
